glosses: (jemanden) mit roher Gewalt durch Schläge mit einem Knüppel niederschlagen

examples.text: „Sie war bei der Demo in Bern und hatte auf einmal Bilder von Südafrika vor Augen, wie die Apartheid-Gegner zusammengeknüppelt wurden.“
„Polizisten hatten die in einer Schule schlafenden Demonstranten, unter ihnen viele Deutsche, überfallen und zusammengeknüppelt.“
„Noch 2006 ließ Lukaschenko Demonstranten zusammenknüppeln und Wahlaufrufe der Opposition von seinen Leuten niederbrüllen.“

translations.source_sense_description: mit roher Gewalt durch Schläge mit einem Knüppel zu Boden bringen

glosses: A short, heavy club, often of wood, which is thicker or loaded at one end.

examples.text: We smashed the radio with a steel bludgeon.

glosses: To strike or hit with something hard, usually on the head; to club.

examples.text: The apprehended rioter was bludgeoned to death.
They didn't get shot to death in hold-ups, strangled to death in rapes, stabbed to death in saloons, bludgeoned to death with axes by parents or children or die summarily by some other act of God.

Thomas Briggs, a senior bank clerk in the City, lived in Hackney, and on 9 July 1864 he was returning there by train from Fenchurch Street after a Saturday spent at work when he was bludgeoned to death in a first-class carriage, probably by a young German tailor named Franz Müller. (Let's hope it was Müller, because he was hanged for it.) And so Briggs was an all-round pioneer: an early commuter and the very first victim of a railway murder.

glosses: To coerce someone, as if with a bludgeon.

examples.text: Their favorite method was bludgeoning us with the same old arguments in favor of their opinions.

Gianna Parasini: You've never worked in the corporate world, have you, Commander? You can't bludgeon through bureaucracy.
Shepard: I can bludgeon pretty hard.
